subject: Harlequin Health — connectivity options for Redwood Private (on-prem/ VPC)
messages:

Subject: Connecting Harlequin on-prem to Redwood Private — quick ask

Jonas,

Thanks for taking this call last week. We pulled together the current network diagrams (attached) and need a concise recommendation from Redwood on which approach to use to connect our on-prem datacenter to a Redwood Private deployment in our AWS account. High level constraints:

- We need <100ms p99 latency for inference requests (regional).
- Typical throughput: 2–5Gbps sustained, bursts to 12Gbps during peak training/eval windows.
- Must be SOC2 / HIPAA-friendly; auditors will verify IP allowlists and encrypted transit.
- Procurement wants a single recommended path to scope the work and budget.

Can you outline tradeoffs between VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN? Attached: harlequin-network-drawings-v2.pdf. Procurement timeline attached as well.

Tom

Infrastructure Lead, Harlequin Health
From: jonas_weber@redwood.ai

Cc: Nora Singh <nora.singh@harlequinhealth.com>, kimberly_park@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 4 May 2026 11:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Connecting Harlequin on-prem to Redwood Private — quick ask

Tom — thanks for the diagrams, that helps. High level summary up front:

- VPC Peering: best for lowest-latency/high-throughput within the same AWS region/account family. Simple networking but you must manage route propagation and endpoint exposure. No transit gateway cost if single-peering, but scales poorly for many VPCs.

- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): good when Harlequin wants a stable, whitelisted endpoint (ENIs) and minimal exposure of our service VPC. Easier for compliance (customer controls ENIs), supports per-service access controls. Slightly higher per-GB cost and extra NAT/ENI management.

- Site-to-site VPN: easiest to onboard for on-prem legacy networks and across cloud providers. Higher latency/variable throughput and additional operational overhead. Good as fallback or temporary method while we set up peering/privatelink.

A couple of clarifying Qs to scope the recommendation:
1) Will you host the Redwood Private data plane in Harlequin's AWS account (customer-managed VPC), or do you want Redwood-managed Private VPCs with controlled peering/links?
2) Do you require single static egress IPs for audit whitelisting?
3) Any regulatory requirement for air-gapped or strict cross-region segregation?

I'll loop Kim from infra to provide concrete throughput/architecture tradeoffs and a recommended pilot pattern.

Next steps: if you confirm answers above we can propose a one-week pilot plan and a roll-out checklist.

— Jonas Weber
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Adding a bit more detail from an infra perspective with Harlequin's constraints in mind.

Peering (recommended for data-plane):
- Pros: native AWS path, minimal extra hops => lowest latency and predictable bandwidth. Good for high-throughput inference traffic if Redwood services are deployed in Harlequin's account or a partner VPC in same region.
- Cons: requires route table management, cross-account peering has limits (no transitive peering), and maintenance during VPC CIDR changes. No integration with AWS PrivateLink security model.

PrivateLink (recommended for control-plane + service endpoints):
- Pros: Customer controls the ENIs; we expose a service behind an NLB in Redwood VPC. Great for access control, avoids exposing our subnets, and easier for auditors because traffic lands on customer-managed ENIs.
- Cons: per-GB charges and ENI scaling considerations under very high connection churn. Slight extra latency compared to peering (tens of ms in worst case).

Site-to-site VPN (fallback/on-ramp):
- Pros: Fastest to set up, supports on-prem devices, and works across cloud providers.
- Cons: Unpredictable latency, throughput limited by VPN device and tunnel configuration. Not ideal as primary for p99 <100ms unless you're co-located.

Suggested hybrid pilot for Harlequin (given your throughput and compliance needs):
1) Control plane & management traffic: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) — gives you whitelisted, auditable endpoints.
2) Data plane (in-region, high-throughput): VPC Peering between Harlequin VPC and Redwood compute VPC hosted in Harlequin's account or peer-compatible account.
3) S2S VPN as backup and for cross-region/burst overflow (encrypted transit while we validate peering).

Operational items: IP whitelisting (we can provide a small set of egress IPs), NATing considerations for callbacks, security group templates, and CloudWatch/Datadog sampling for latency SLO verification.

I can draft a one-page action checklist for procurement and netops if you want.

— Kimberly Park
Senior Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

- Does Redwood support an architecture that places compute in our account (so peering is intra-account) vs Redwood hosting in a partner account? Which do you prefer?
- Also, do you have guidance on using AWS Network Firewall or Transit Gateway in this pattern — procurement is asking about scale and security controls.

I've attached the procurement timeline (harlequin-procurement-timeline.pdf). We are targeting a pilot start in the first week of June.

Tom
From: jonas_weber@redwood.ai

Subject: Re: Connecting Harlequin on-prem to Redwood Private — quick ask

Tom — finalizing the proposal and action items so procurement/netops have a clear path. Short answers:

1) Static egress IPs: yes — we can provision a small set of NAT IPs for callbacks and admin traffic. If you host compute in your account, you control those IPs directly; if Redwood hosts compute in a partner VPC, we can allocate static egress IPs (we'll document them and rotate on a maintenance window).

2) Preferred hosting model: for lowest latency and simplest data-plane scale, we prefer deploying Redwood compute into your AWS account (customer-managed VPC). That lets you peer directly and keeps data plane under your governance. If that's not desirable, we can host in a Redwood-managed VPC and use PrivateLink + peering with cross-account patterns. We'll note costs for each in the pilot doc.

3) Transit Gateway & Network Firewall:
- Transit Gateway: useful if you have many VPCs to connect or want central routing. Adds cost but simplifies route scale. If Harlequin intends to connect multiple environment VPCs (dev/stage/prod), recommend TGW.
- Network Firewall: recommended if you need centralized L7 controls or stateful inspection beyond security groups — place it in-line in the data path or as inspection VPC.

Proposed pilot (week of 2026-06-01):
- Phase 0 (2 days): Confirm CIDRs, whitelists, and procurement signoff.
- Phase 1 (3 days): Stand up PrivateLink for control-plane endpoints; validate auth and IAM flows.
- Phase 2 (5 days): Deploy Redwood compute in Harlequin account, establish VPC Peering for data plane, run synthetic p99 latency tests and throughput soak.
- Phase 3 (ongoing): Enable S2S VPN as fallback and test failover.

Action items:
- Harlequin: confirm AWS account ID(s), CIDR ranges, and preferred contact for NetOps (Nora?).
- Redwood: provide one-page network runbook, list of static egress IPs, and pilot resource estimate.

I'll share the pilot runbook and a HubSpot update (deal HQL-498) by Friday. If that works, I'll open a DocuSign PO template link for procurement.
